title: Solar System B study guide
deck: 2027 • A visual investigation of habitability within and beyond our Solar System

visual.caption: An illustrated field guide for learning, comparing and reasoning.

panels: The central question
Where could life as we know it find usable water, energy, and chemistry for long enough to function? Follow clues in rocks, spectra, atmospheres, and distant worlds to build and test an explanation.
How to use the guide

Read a page, cover its explanation, then answer the question at the bottom aloud. Sketch the diagram from memory. Compare worlds by the same criteria. Use the worked relationships to explain changes without a calculator.
question: What would you need to know before calling a world “habitable”? Name three kinds of evidence, not three objects.
answer: Look for a usable solvent, accessible chemistry and sustained usable energy, together with conditions and duration compatible with known biology. Evidence might include water-related geology, chemical composition and an energy source.

title: A clue is not a verdict
deck: Separate a measurement from an interpretation and an extraordinary claim.

visual.caption: Habitability ≠ inhabited. Organic molecules ≠ organisms.

panels: Build a chain of reasoning

An absorption feature can indicate a molecule. A molecule may indicate a process. That process could have biological or nonbiological causes. State what was measured, what assumptions connect the steps, and what else could explain the result.
Ask what would change your mind

A good explanation makes a testable prediction. Combine independent clues: morphology plus minerals, gravity plus magnetic response, or a spectrum plus atmospheric models. A non-detection limits what an instrument could have seen; it does not prove universal absence.
question: A spectrum contains methane. Give one reason that this alone cannot demonstrate life.
answer: Methane can have nonbiological sources. Its context, source rates, losses and independent measurements must be examined.

classification: Supporting foundation, not an extra enumerated rule requirement
title: Where are the named worlds?
deck: Start with what each object is, what it orbits and the scale of the system.

rows: Rocky planet; second planet from the Sun
Rocky planet; fourth planet from the Sun
Dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune
visual.caption: Rounded teaching scales, not ephemerides or a list of mandatory memorization values.

panels: Read the hierarchy

Venus and Mars are rocky planets. Makemake is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune, not a moon. Bennu is a near-Earth asteroid: it still orbits the Sun, not Earth. The phrase Jupiter-family comet describes a dynamical family, not a moon of Jupiter. These distinctions locate the evidence before asking about habitability.
Keep size separate from orbit

One astronomical unit, AU, is about 150 million kilometers, approximately Earth’s mean Sun distance. A body’s diameter is its full width through the center, twice its radius. Orbital separation is a different quantity. The values here are rounded comparative scales; distances change along eccentric orbits. An irregular comet does not have the same simple spherical diameter as a nearly round planet.
question: Why does “near-Earth asteroid” not mean that Bennu is Earth’s moon?
answer: Bennu orbits the Sun. Near-Earth describes the proximity of its solar orbit to Earth’s orbital neighborhood.

classification: Supporting foundation, not an extra enumerated rule requirement
title: Moons: two orbital scales at once
deck: Jupiter hosts Ganymede and Europa; Saturn hosts Enceladus and Titan.

visual.caption: Rounded teaching scales, not ephemerides or a list of mandatory memorization values.

panels: A moon’s parent matters

A moon travels around its planet while that whole system travels around the Sun. Jupiter’s solar orbital scale is about 5.2 AU; Saturn’s is about 9.6 AU. Use the planet-centered distance for a simple planetary tide or orbital calculation, and the Sun-centered distance for incoming sunlight. Do not substitute one for the other. Distances listed here are approximate center-to-center orbital scales, not heights above cloud tops.
Name the comparison class

Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System by diameter. Titan is Saturn’s largest moon and the Solar System’s second-largest moon. Enceladus is only about one tenth Titan’s diameter. At roughly 500 km across, Enceladus is about a thousand times wider than the roughly 500 m asteroid Bennu. Convert units before judging whether objects are comparable.
question: Which distance controls Europa’s solar illumination: its orbit around Jupiter or the Jupiter system’s orbit around the Sun?
answer: The Jupiter system’s distance from the Sun controls solar illumination. Europa’s distance from Jupiter matters for its planetary orbit and tidal forcing.

classification: Supporting foundation, not an extra enumerated rule requirement
title: Orbit size and shape
deck: Separate the size of a world from the size and shape of its orbit.

rows: A distance unit of about 150 million km, approximately Earth’s mean distance from the Sun. It is a length, not a time.
Radius runs from center to surface; diameter runs across the whole body through its center and is twice the radius.
Half the longest diameter of an elliptical orbit. It specifies orbital size; it is not the changing instantaneous distance between the orbiting bodies.
A measure of how much an orbit departs from a circle: e = 0 is circular; 0 < e < 1 is elliptical.
visual.caption: Use radius and semimajor axis for different physical lengths.

panels: Orbit size is not object size
A planet’s radius describes the planet. Its semimajor axis describes its orbit. Keep the two lengths separate when using an equation.
Sketch it
Draw a circle and an ellipse. Mark the center, the two foci of the ellipse, and the semimajor axis. Put the star at one focus, not at the center.
question: A moon’s diameter is 3,000 km and its orbital semimajor axis is 400,000 km. Which length tells you its radius? What does the other describe?
answer: The radius is half the diameter, so 1,500 km. The semimajor axis describes the size of the orbit, not the size of the moon. For a circular orbit it equals the center-to-center orbital distance.

classification: Supporting foundation, not an extra enumerated rule requirement
title: Rotation and resonance
deck: Rotation describes a body turning; revolution describes its motion around another body.

rows: The nearest and farthest orbital points from the central body. For an orbit around the Sun they are perihelion and aphelion.

A repeating ratio between orbital periods, allowing repeated gravitational interactions. Ganymede:Europa:Io complete 1:2:4 orbits in the same time; those repeated interactions can maintain eccentricity.
Rotation period equals orbital period, so approximately the same hemisphere faces the body being orbited. This does not mean the moon never rotates.
A region of many icy bodies beyond Neptune’s orbit; Makemake is a member.
visual.caption: Compare time intervals carefully: orbital period and rotation period describe different motions.

panels: A moon can rotate and keep one face toward its planet
During one orbit, a synchronously rotating moon also turns once about its axis. From the planet, roughly the same hemisphere stays in view.
Count the orbits
While Ganymede completes one orbit, Europa completes two and Io completes four. Repeated gravitational interactions can keep the orbits slightly noncircular.
question: A synchronously rotating moon keeps one face toward its planet. How many times does it rotate during one complete orbit?
answer: It rotates once. Mark a spot facing the planet and follow the moon through four positions around its orbit: that marked direction must turn through one complete rotation to keep pointing inward. A moon that did not rotate would show different faces to its planet.

classification: Supporting foundation, not an extra enumerated rule requirement
title: Names and scales
deck: Names describe relationships. They do not prove a world is Earth-like.

rows: A nearly round body orbiting the Sun that has not gravitationally cleared its orbital neighborhood and is not a satellite. It is not simply any small planet or large moon.

An exoplanet orbits a star other than the Sun; its host star is the star it orbits. In these system names the lowercase suffix identifies a planet, for example Kepler-452 b rather than the star Kepler-452.
An angular unit equal to 1/3,600 degree; an angular separation is not a physical distance.
A distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arcsecond; about 3.26 light-years. This definition explains separation(AU)/distance(parsecs) = angle(arcseconds) for small angles.
visual.caption: A shared star connects a planetary system, not every planet’s conditions.

panels: Name the object
Kepler-452 names the star. Kepler-452 b names its planet. Makemake is a dwarf planet orbiting our Sun; it is not a moon.
Angle is not distance
Two planets can have the same projected separation from their stars but look closer together when the systems are farther away. At 10 parsecs, a projected separation of 1 AU spans 0.1 arcsecond.
question: Does sharing a star mean two planets have the same temperature? Does the name Kepler-452b mean that it orbits a planet called Kepler-452?
answer: No. Distance, atmosphere, albedo and internal heat can differ even around the same star. Kepler-452 is the star; the lower-case b designates a planet in that stellar system, not a moon orbiting a planet.

classification: Supporting foundation, not an extra enumerated rule requirement
title: Chemistry and surfaces
deck: Connect composition and physical processes to a specific observation.

rows: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different neutron numbers. D/H compares deuterium (heavy hydrogen) with ordinary hydrogen; it is a chemical-history tracer, not a unique label of origin.
Internal heating from radioactive decay; distinct from tidal heating caused by changing deformation.
An atmosphere supplied or replenished by processes such as outgassing, rather than simply retained primordial nebular gas. The term does not mean a confirmed Earth-like atmosphere.
An extremely tenuous gas environment around a surface, unlike a thick collisional atmosphere such as Titan’s. Oxygen in such an environment is not breathable air or proof of life.
visual.caption: Ask which material or process could produce the measured signal.

panels: A chemical fingerprint is a clue
D/H is a ratio of two hydrogen isotopes. Similar ratios can support a shared history, but processing can change a ratio and different sources may overlap.
Keep origins separate
Radiogenic heat comes from radioactive decay. Tidal heat comes from changing deformation. Both can heat an interior, but they have different energy sources.
question: How could a chemical tracer help identify material escaping from an interior without proving that life is present?
answer: A tracer’s composition may connect surface or plume material to a plausible interior source. For example, salts in expelled ice can support contact with salty water. That inference concerns origin and transport; it is not, by itself, evidence of organisms.

title: Four requirements that interact
deck: A world can satisfy one requirement while failing another.
panels: Ingredients must be accessible

Liquid water is the known solvent for cellular chemistry. Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur supply major biological ingredients. Merely having these elements is not enough: their chemical forms and transport determine whether organisms could use them.
Energy must be usable over time

Light or chemical reactions can drive metabolism. A stable environment need not be gentle, but its conditions must allow molecules, membranes and reactions to work. Look for sustained energy gradients and enough time, not simply a warm temperature at one instant.
question: An ocean contains nutrients but no usable energy gradient. Which requirement is missing, and why is “lots of water” not sufficient?
answer: A usable energy source is missing. Water permits reactions but does not guarantee an energy-yielding reaction or a continuing supply of reactants.

title: Liquid water needs the right conditions
deck: Temperature alone does not tell you whether water can remain liquid.
panels: Read a phase diagram

A phase diagram maps the stable form of a substance against temperature and pressure. Cross a boundary and the stable phase changes. At low pressure, exposed ice may sublime directly to vapor. At sufficiently high pressure, liquid water can exist above its familiar boiling point at Earth’s sea level.
Apply it to a world

Mars has a thin atmosphere, so persistent exposed pure liquid water is difficult today. Beneath ice or rock, pressure and insulation change the problem. A subsurface ocean can therefore exist on a world whose exposed surface is much too cold for liquid water.
question: Why might an icy moon hold liquid water underneath a frozen surface? Explain both pressure and energy.
answer: Overlying material provides pressure and insulation. Internal heating can balance heat loss and maintain liquid below a cold surface. Pressure alone does not provide the required heat.

title: Ice is not just one material
deck: Structure, impurities and trapped gases change what “water present” means.
panels: Compare solid structures

Crystalline ice has an ordered molecular arrangement. Amorphous ice lacks long-range order and can form under very cold conditions or through irradiation. A clathrate is a water-ice framework containing guest molecules such as methane. Trapped gas is not a liquid ocean.
Brines change the limits

Dissolved salts can lower the freezing point, allowing liquid at lower temperatures than pure water. But very salty solutions reduce water activity, making water less available for biology. “Liquid exists” and “life can use that liquid” are different claims.
question: A salt-rich liquid remains unfrozen below 0°C. Why does that not automatically make it a good habitat?
answer: Salt can lower freezing temperature while lowering water activity. Temperature, acidity and other constraints may still prevent metabolism.

title: The molecules that cells build
deck: These are models from known Earth life, not requirements proven for all possible life.
panels: Information and machinery

Proteins are chains of amino acids folded into structures that can catalyze reactions, transport material and support cells. DNA and RNA are nucleic acids built from nucleotides; they store and transmit information, and some RNA molecules also catalyze reactions.
Boundaries and resources

Many lipids have water-attracting and water-avoiding regions, helping membranes form. Carbohydrates include sugars used in energy transfer and structural materials. Finding amino acids or nucleobases reveals useful chemistry; it does not show that a cell assembled them.
question: What is the difference between finding amino acids and finding a functioning protein-based organism?
answer: Amino acids are ingredients. A functioning organism requires organized machinery, information, boundaries and energy use; nonbiological chemistry can make amino acids.

title: Extreme does not mean impossible
deck: Earth organisms widen the search, but they do not erase physical limits.
panels: Living on chemical energy

A chemolithoautotroph obtains energy by oxidizing inorganic substances and uses carbon dioxide as a carbon source. Near a hydrothermal vent, rock-water reactions can supply reduced chemicals; mixing with other water can provide electron acceptors. The useful habitat may be the mixing zone, not the hottest fluid.
Survival is not growth

Some tardigrades enter a dehydrated, very low-metabolism state that tolerates stresses lethal to many animals. Surviving an exposure, later recovering, and continuously reproducing in that environment are different tests. Conditions that allow a dormant traveler need not allow an ecosystem.
question: Would surviving ten days in vacuum prove an organism could live and reproduce on an airless moon? Why not?
answer: No. Dormant survival followed by recovery under favorable conditions does not demonstrate continuous metabolism or reproduction in vacuum.

title: Life can exploit disequilibrium
deck: A chemical energy source is a reaction that has somewhere to go.
panels: A gradient can power chemistry

Chemical disequilibrium means a mixture has not reached its equilibrium composition. Certain reactions can release usable energy as reactants move toward equilibrium. Hydrogen from rock-water reactions can be an electron donor; other chemicals can accept electrons. Organisms couple favorable reactions to cellular work.
A biosignature needs context

Methane and oxidants together may suggest continual replenishment, but geology, sunlight and atmospheric escape can also maintain disequilibrium. Reaction rates matter: a thermodynamically favored reaction may proceed slowly. Look for supply, transport and compatible conditions, not a single “magic” molecule.
question: If a chemical fuel is consumed faster than it is replenished, what happens to the long-term habitat?
answer: The usable chemical imbalance is depleted. A sustained habitat requires replenishment or another source of usable energy.

title: The habitable zone is a starting point
deck: The usual stellar habitable zone concerns surface liquid water on a suitable planet.
panels: Distance sets incoming energy

Stellar luminosity and orbital distance determine received flux. A brighter star places the comparable-flux region farther out. The zone is not a painted ring with universal edges: atmosphere, clouds, surface reflectivity and greenhouse warming affect the result.
Habitats can exist outside it

Europa and Enceladus motivate a different question: can internal energy maintain water under ice? Tidal and radiogenic heating can matter where sunlight is weak. Conversely, a planet inside the stellar zone can be dry, airless or otherwise unsuitable. “In the zone” does not mean “Earth-like.”
question: Why is a subsurface ocean on a distant moon not a contradiction of the surface-water habitable-zone idea?
answer: The conventional zone addresses surface liquid water under suitable atmospheric conditions. An internally heated, insulated ocean is a different setting.
prerequisite_note: Radiogenic heating means heat released by radioactive decay.

title: An atmosphere changes the heat budget
deck: Absorbing infrared radiation alters how a surface loses energy to space.
panels: Follow the energy

A world absorbs some incoming starlight and reflects the rest. Its surface and atmosphere emit thermal radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and emit selected infrared wavelengths. The surface temperature adjusts as the whole system balances incoming and outgoing energy.
Keep the quantities separate

Albedo measures reflected light, not greenhouse strength. Equilibrium temperature is a simple radiative benchmark, not automatically surface temperature. Venus illustrates how a bright, reflective world can still have an extremely hot surface beneath a massive greenhouse atmosphere.
question: Can increasing reflectivity cool a planet while increasing greenhouse opacity warms its surface? Explain why these are different processes.
answer: Yes. Higher albedo reduces absorbed starlight, while infrared opacity changes radiative cooling and can warm the surface. They affect different parts of the energy budget.

title: Can a world keep its atmosphere?
deck: Gravity, molecular mass, temperature and stellar activity all matter.
panels: Compare escape and motion

Escape speed grows with the square root of mass divided by radius. Gas particles have a distribution of speeds; lighter particles move faster at the same temperature. A hot, low-gravity world loses light gases more readily than a cold, high-gravity world, all else equal.
Thermal escape is not the whole story

Ultraviolet light can heat or dissociate gases. Stellar winds and ion processes can remove particles. Impacts, volcanism and chemistry can add or remove atmosphere. A magnetic field is not a simple yes/no habitability shield: retention is an evolving balance of several processes.
question: Why can hydrogen escape more readily than carbon dioxide from the same upper atmosphere?
answer: At the same temperature, lighter molecules have higher typical thermal speeds. More hydrogen particles can reach escape-capable speeds, all else equal.

title: Tides turn changing shape into heat
deck: The key is a difference in gravity across a body, not simply strong gravity.
panels: Stretching is differential gravity

The near side of a moon feels a stronger pull than its far side. Changes in the tidal deformation can dissipate mechanical energy as heat. Orbital eccentricity and interactions with other moons can maintain the changing stress; a static bulge alone does not imply continual heating.
Connect heat to habitability

Internal heat can help sustain liquid beneath ice and promote rock-water chemistry. Too little heat can freeze a habitat; intense heating can also be destructive. The tidal acceleration scale changes approximately as planet mass × moon radius ÷ separation cubed.
question: If separation doubles while the other quantities stay fixed, how does the tidal acceleration scale change?
answer: The tidal acceleration scale falls to one eighth. Heating power is not determined by this scaling alone.
prerequisite_note: Orbital eccentricity measures departure from a circle; repeated orbital-period ratios, called resonances, can sustain gravitational interactions.

title: Landforms preserve a history
deck: A shape is evidence of a process, but one shape can have more than one explanation.
panels: Work from pattern to process

Branching valleys may record runoff. A delta forms where flowing material enters a body of standing water and deposits sediment. Layering records repeated deposition or other changes. Compare the geometry with mineral composition, surrounding terrain and relative ages.
Distinguish past from present

An ancient lakebed demonstrates a past environment, not a present lake. Hydrated minerals can preserve water-rock interaction after water is gone. Fractures, youthful surfaces and cryovolcanic deposits may suggest internal activity, but composition and heat-flow evidence strengthen the interpretation.
question: What additional observation would strengthen the claim that a fan-shaped feature is a river delta rather than a dry landslide deposit?
answer: Supporting evidence could include channels feeding the feature, sediment layers consistent with deposition in standing water, and water-related minerals in the right geological context.

title: Spectra turn light into chemistry
deck: Molecules interact with particular wavelengths, leaving patterns in light.
panels: Identify a pattern, not one dip

A reflected-light spectrum can contain absorption bands from surface minerals or atmospheric gases. Compare several bands with laboratory or modeled spectra. Band strength depends on abundance, temperature, grain size, path length and mixtures, not abundance alone.
Ask what the instrument sees

A thermal spectrum probes emitted radiation. A transit spectrum compares a planet’s apparent size at different wavelengths as starlight passes through its limb. Clouds, hazes, instrument noise and stellar activity can imitate or hide features. A flat spectrum does not uniquely identify an airless planet.
question: Why is matching several absorption bands stronger evidence than identifying a single low point in a noisy spectrum?
answer: Several correctly placed bands are harder to reproduce accidentally and constrain a molecular identification better than one feature, especially with noise and mixtures.

title: Venus: temperature is not the whole test
deck: A world can have a comfortable-temperature layer and still lack conditions that known life requires.

visual.name: Venus
visual.caption: Atmospheric profile, not to scale. Cloud temperature alone does not establish habitability.

panels: Read the environment

Venus is a rocky planet, second from the Sun, with an orbital scale of about 0.72 AU. Venus resembles Earth in size, but its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere produces a very different surface environment. The ground is about 467 °C, beneath pressure roughly 93 times Earth’s sea-level pressure. Strong atmospheric absorption and emission of infrared radiation help explain the heat.

Higher clouds have milder temperatures and pressures. That makes them scientifically interesting, not automatically habitable. Surface and cloud environments must be evaluated separately.
Test the chemistry

Venus’s cloud droplets contain concentrated sulfuric acid, not ordinary rainwater. Their very low water activity means little water is available for the chemistry of known organisms. Temperature, solvent chemistry, acidity, usable energy, and persistence all matter together.

Whether early Venus ever sustained an ocean remains uncertain. Reported phosphine is disputed, and a molecular signal would still require reliable identification and evaluation of nonbiological sources before supporting a life claim.
question: Why would finding an Earth-like cloud temperature be insufficient evidence of a habitable environment?
answer: Temperature is only one constraint. Investigators must also establish suitable solvent availability, chemistry, energy, and conditions that persist long enough.

title: Mars: distinguish a past habitat from present life
deck: Geology preserves clues to ancient water, while today’s surface presents different environmental challenges.

visual.name: Mars
visual.caption: Past lakes are geological reconstructions. Their existence does not demonstrate that organisms lived there.

panels: Reconstruct the past

Mars is a rocky planet, fourth from the Sun, at about 1.5 AU and about half Earth’s diameter. Valleys, deltas, layered sediments, and water-altered minerals support ancient liquid-water environments on Mars. Different clues answer different questions: a delta suggests deposition where a stream entered standing water; altered minerals record chemical interaction with water.

Fine lake sediments can preserve organic compounds and environmental context. An ancient habitable lake means conditions could support life as we understand it, not that life actually developed there.
Keep the present separate

Modern Mars has a thin, mostly carbon-dioxide atmosphere, with typical surface pressure around 0.6% of Earth’s. Stable exposed liquid water is difficult to maintain. Polar and subsurface ice are water reservoirs, but ice alone is not a liquid-water habitat.

Perseverance’s Cheyava Falls findings were described in 2025 as potential biosignatures. Their origin remains unresolved. Atmospheric escape measurements help explain environmental change, but no single mechanism explains every part of Mars’s history.
question: Why is an ancient lake-bed sample scientifically stronger than an organic molecule detected without geological context?
answer: The lake-bed sample connects chemistry to a reconstructed environment and a plausible preservation setting. An isolated organic molecule can have many nonbiological origins.

title: Ganymede: an ocean inside a layered world
deck: A hidden ocean matters most when we ask how water, rock, and chemical energy could interact.

visual.name: Ganymede
layers: Inferred liquid and high-pressure ice layers
visual.caption: Schematic interior model, not to scale. The arrangement and connectivity of liquid layers remain uncertain.

panels: Follow the magnetic evidence

Ganymede orbits Jupiter and is the largest moon in the entire Solar System by diameter. Galileo discovered its intrinsic magnetic field, while other magnetic and auroral measurements support an electrically conducting interior layer interpreted as salty water.

Do not merge those observations into one claim: the intrinsic field and the ocean’s induced magnetic response are different phenomena. Electrical conductivity helps infer material properties; it does not identify organisms or measure an ocean’s complete chemistry.
Ask whether liquid reaches rock

Deep pressure can stabilize ice phases denser than liquid water. Interior models therefore permit complicated arrangements of rock, high-pressure ice, and liquid. Some arrangements allow water-rock contact; others place substantial ice between the principal ocean and rock.

That distinction affects chemical exchange and possible energy sources. Juno detected surface salts and organic compounds whose distribution may reflect interior brines. The transport route, detailed ocean structure, and biological relevance remain inferred or unknown.
question: Why can two models containing the same amount of water imply different prospects for habitability?
answer: Water’s state and arrangement matter. A liquid layer isolated by high-pressure ice may exchange chemicals with rock differently from an ocean touching a rocky seafloor.

title: Europa: connect the surface to the ocean
deck: A promising ocean requires more than liquid water: ingredients and usable energy must reach the same environment.

visual.name: Europa
visual.caption: Schematic, not to scale. Ocean and interior structure are inferred; transport arrows and hydrothermal activity are hypotheses.

panels: Build the habitability chain

Europa is one of Jupiter’s moons. Europa’s fractured icy surface and magnetic evidence strongly support an ocean beneath the ice. The ocean is expected to contact rock, making water-rock reactions a possible source of useful chemistry. Tidal deformation supplies heat, but heat and metabolic energy are not interchangeable.

Radiation can damage exposed organic compounds while also producing reactive chemicals at the surface. Whether those materials reach the ocean is a separate, crucial question.
Read thickness estimates carefully

Juno microwave data support a conductive ice layer tens of kilometers thick in the observed region. A pure-water-ice model gives 29 ± 10 km; salt and a possible deeper convective layer change the interpretation. This is not a global, exact total thickness.

Webb mapped carbon dioxide in young terrain, favoring an internal source. That links carbon to geological activity without detecting life. Europa Clipper investigates habitability, not a guaranteed answer about organisms.
question: Why should a cross-section show uncertain surface-to-ocean arrows rather than a confirmed open circulation loop?
answer: Surface chemicals and an ocean are supported separately. Their transport rates, pathways, and survival through the ice have not been established as a complete circulation system.

title: Enceladus: sample the plume, question the source
deck: Erupting material gives scientists unusual access to chemistry associated with an ocean beneath an icy shell.

visual.name: Enceladus
visual.caption: Schematic, not to scale. Plume constituents were measured; deep chemical processes are inferred from them.

panels: Separate ingredients from life

Enceladus is a small icy moon of Saturn. Cassini sampled water vapor and ice grains emerging from south-polar fractures. Salts and other measurements strongly support an ocean feeding the plume. Organics reveal carbon chemistry, while phosphate detections add an important biological nutrient to the known inventory.

These discoveries strengthen the case for investigating habitability. They do not establish living cells, a complete biological food supply, or the origin of every detected compound.
Separate heat from chemical energy

Tidal dissipation can help maintain liquid water. Molecular hydrogen in the plume supports water-rock interactions that could create chemical disequilibrium. On Earth, some microbes exploit reactions involving hydrogen and carbon dioxide; applying that analogy here remains hypothetical.

Plume sampling also has limitations. Freezing, transport, concentration, and instrument sensitivity can change which materials are detected. A plume measurement is not automatically a complete, unbiased sample of the entire ocean or seafloor.
question: What is one advantage and one limitation of sampling a plume instead of drilling into an ocean?
answer: A spacecraft can reach erupted material without drilling. However, eruption, freezing, transport, and instrument selection may bias the sampled chemistry.

title: Titan: familiar weather, unfamiliar liquid
deck: Titan’s surface liquid cycle resembles Earth’s in its processes, not in its solvent or biological implications.

visual.name: Titan
visual.caption: Observed surface processes, schematically arranged. Surface lakes contain hydrocarbons, not ordinary liquid water.

panels: Compare physical cycles

Titan orbits Saturn and is the Solar System’s second-largest moon, after Ganymede. Its surface pressure is roughly 1.5 times Earth’s sea-level pressure. Its dense nitrogen-rich atmosphere contains methane, which can evaporate, form clouds, fall as rain, and flow into lakes and seas containing methane and ethane. These processes resemble Earth’s water cycle, but use different liquids. Near −179 °C, water ice forms solid ground rather than ordinary surface lakes.
Organic does not mean biological

Ultraviolet light and energetic particles drive reactions involving atmospheric nitrogen and methane. These reactions build more complex organic compounds and contribute to the haze and surface deposits. Biological activity is not required.

Hypothetical life using liquid hydrocarbons remains speculative: no known terrestrial organism uses methane as its cellular solvent. Models of cell-like compartments explore chemical possibilities, not observed cells. Dragonfly will investigate how far Titan’s prebiotic chemistry has progressed without assuming a living biosphere.
question: How can Titan have lakes while still being too cold for ordinary liquid-water lakes at its surface?
answer: Its lakes use different substances. Methane and ethane can be liquid under Titan’s conditions, while water is predominantly solid ice.

deck: The surface methane cycle is observed; Titan’s deeper water-rich structure must be inferred from geophysical measurements.

visual.name: Titan interior
visual.caption: Two proposed interiors, not measured cross-sections: an ocean-bearing model and a December 2025 slushy-ice model. Their layer boundaries and liquid connections remain uncertain.

panels: Observation first, model second

Cassini’s tracking measurements constrain how Titan responds to Saturn’s tides. A large deformation had supported a buried-ocean interpretation. A December 2025 reanalysis also measured strong tidal dissipation and found that its tested global-ocean models could not fit the combined response.

A slushy high-pressure ice model performed better. This is evidence-driven revision of an interior model, not a spacecraft seeing directly beneath the surface. Independent tests and improved material physics remain important.
Keep separate water settings

Possible melt pockets in the revised interior model are not proof of an ocean, a habitat, or life. Their locations, connections, and chemical conditions are not directly sampled. Nor does the new interpretation establish that Titan contains no liquid water anywhere.

Another setting is transient liquid water produced by impacts. Such melting could mix water with complex surface organics. Dragonfly’s investigation of surface materials can address prebiotic processes even while the deeper interior remains uncertain.
question: Why should a revised interior model not erase the separately observed evidence for Titan’s surface lakes?
answer: The two claims concern different places and substances. Surface hydrocarbon lakes are observed; the debated interior concerns subsurface water and ice.

title: Makemake: reading the chemistry of a distant world
deck: Remote chemistry constrains this distant dwarf planet while leaving much of its interior and history unresolved.

visual.name: Makemake
visual.caption: Do not depict a known subsurface ocean. Interior shading indicates missing information, not measured layers.

panels: Establish what is observed

Makemake is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune. Makemake lies in the Kuiper Belt, averaging about 46 times Earth’s distance from the Sun. Its surface contains methane and ethane ice. At this distance, sunlight is much weaker than near Earth, and the surface is extremely cold.

JWST work reported gaseous methane fluorescence. The investigators considered a tenuous bound atmosphere and escaping gas, but neither model fully reproduced the observations. A particular atmosphere or plume geometry is therefore not uniquely established.
Compare explanations, not headlines

Methane isotope ratios can constrain the molecule’s origin. One analysis favored production associated with internal heating and rock chemistry; another showed that inherited primordial methane could explain the ratios under different assumptions.

The correct lesson is a chain of increasingly model-dependent inference: identify molecules, estimate isotope ratios, then compare origin scenarios. These results do not uniquely demonstrate an active ocean or hydrothermal vents. Cold surface ice and possible internal activity also represent different environments with different habitability questions.
question: Why does detecting methane on Makemake not demonstrate either life or a present-day subsurface ocean?
answer: Methane has nonbiological and inherited origins. Its detection alone does not uniquely establish its production mechanism, interior structure, or the existence of liquid water.

title: Bennu: a sample of ancient chemistry
deck: Returned material reveals ancient chemical processing and life’s ingredients without demonstrating organisms or assembled biological machinery.

visual.name: Bennu
visual.caption: Bennu is a roughly 500-meter-wide, top-shaped rubble pile. Ancient water-related processing occurred in its larger parent body; this is not a present-day ocean.

panels: Read the returned sample

Bennu is a near-Earth, carbon-rich asteroid about 500 meters across that orbits the Sun. OSIRIS-REx delivered Bennu material to Earth in September 2023. Laboratory analysis can identify molecules and minerals in detail, while careful curation helps distinguish extraterrestrial chemistry from contamination. Bennu itself is a small rubble-pile asteroid, not a planet with a thick atmosphere.

Analyses identified many amino acids and all five canonical nucleobases. Later work reported sugars including ribose and glucose. These are chemical ingredients, not detected proteins, DNA, RNA, or cells.
Reconstruct the parent body

Salt minerals and water-altered material record ancient aqueous processing associated with Bennu’s larger parent body. Heating, water-rock reactions, brine evolution, disruption, and reassembly belong to a reconstructed history; they should not be illustrated as water currently flowing inside Bennu.

Asteroids can help explain how organic compounds and water-bearing material reached early planets. Delivery of ingredients is not the same as delivery of living organisms, and it does not by itself explain every chemical step leading to life.
question: What is the difference between finding nucleobases in a sample and finding DNA in that sample?
answer: Nucleobases are components. DNA requires organized nucleotides linked into a polymer; finding separate building blocks does not demonstrate that assembled molecule or an organism.

title: 67P: frozen ingredients can travel
deck: A comet can preserve water and organic chemistry without providing a stable liquid-water habitat.

visual.name: 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko
visual.caption: Schematic nucleus and coma. The coma is escaping material, not a dense, stable planetary atmosphere.

panels: Follow the material

67P is a Jupiter-family comet that orbits the Sun about every 6.5 years; the family name does not mean it orbits Jupiter. Rosetta studied comet 67P at close range. As solar heating increases, volatile ices release gas and help drive dust activity. Sublimation changes a solid directly into gas; a visible coma does not require a liquid-water ocean inside the nucleus.

ROSINA detected glycine, the simplest amino acid, and phosphorus in the coma. Such measurements support comets as reservoirs and potential carriers of prebiotic ingredients, not as demonstrated inhabited worlds.
Interpret chemical fingerprints

Molecular oxygen was also detected. Its presence shows why chemical context matters: oxygen can have nonbiological explanations, so its detection alone is not proof of photosynthesis.

The hydrogen-isotope ratio D/H can help compare cometary water with terrestrial water. Different reanalyses of 67P have reached competing conclusions about the ratio and its variability. The useful question is how sampling, release physics, and measurement models affect the comparison, not whether one comet proves or disproves all cometary delivery of Earth’s water.
question: Why does detecting water vapor around a comet fail to establish a liquid-water habitat?
answer: The vapor can originate through sublimation of ice. A habitat requires suitable liquid conditions, chemistry, energy, and persistence, none of which follows from vapor alone.
