title: TRAPPIST-1: seven planets, seven experiments
deck: A shared star enables comparison, but similar size and habitable-zone location do not establish Earth-like conditions.

visual.name: TRAPPIST-1
labels: e, f, g in common HZ models
visual.caption: Use separate scales for orbital distance and planet size. Planet surfaces must be labeled artistic hypotheses.

panels: Explain the compact system

Seven approximately Earth-size planets orbit the small, faint star TRAPPIST-1. All have orbits smaller than Mercury’s around the Sun, yet some receive irradiation compatible with commonly modeled surface-water habitable zones because their star is much dimmer.

A habitable zone assumes suitable atmospheric and water conditions. It does not guarantee either. Planets e, f, and g are useful targets, not confirmed oceans or seven interchangeable versions of Earth.
Use the system as a comparison

A small star gives a relatively large planet-to-star area ratio, making transits easier to measure. Short orbital periods also allow repeated observations. Those advantages are balanced by stellar flares, spots, and bright regions that complicate atmospheric measurements.

Close orbits make synchronous rotation plausible. A permanent day side does not automatically prohibit habitability: an atmosphere or ocean could transport heat, if present. Different irradiation levels, volatile histories, and atmospheric loss prevent an inner planet’s result from answering for the entire system.
question: Why can a planet orbiting closer than Mercury still lie in a modeled habitable zone around another star?
answer: Received energy depends on stellar luminosity as well as distance. A much fainter star’s habitable zone lies much closer to it.

title: TRAPPIST-1: what do the measurements allow?
deck: Atmosphere searches compare models against noisy data; neither a flat spectrum nor a good fit supplies a unique answer.

visual.name: TRAPPIST-1 atmosphere evidence
rows: Thermal data disfavor tested thick, heat-redistributing atmospheres.
Not a result for all seven planets
Limits depend on models and data treatment
Do not substitute another planet’s result
visual.caption: Dated evidence summary through 23 October 2026. Excluding a tested model is not excluding every atmosphere.

panels: Match the technique to the question

Transmission spectroscopy measures how the apparent transit depth changes with wavelength. Absorption features can constrain gases, while high clouds or a compact heavy atmosphere can weaken those features. Stellar surface variations can also mimic a planetary signal.

Thermal observations address another question: how much infrared radiation emerges from different orbital phases? Day-night contrasts help constrain heat redistribution, but the interpretation still depends on atmospheric and surface models.
Keep each result bounded

The b/c infrared observations favor little heat transfer from day to night. Airless surfaces fit well, although some thin or weak-greenhouse atmosphere models remain possible. For e, a secondary atmosphere remains unresolved. An analysis published in 2026 of five f transits observed in 2022–2023 disfavors tested extended hydrogen/helium atmospheres. Heavier atmospheres are harder to constrain, and results depend on how the data and the star’s changing light are modeled.

Flares occurred during all five f observing visits. Not detecting one kind of stellar contamination does not mean the star was quiet. No established atmospheric composition or ocean follows for g or h from the evidence summarized here. A result for one planet is not a system-wide verdict.
question: Give two explanations for a nearly flat transmission spectrum besides a bare, airless planet.
answer: A high-mean-molecular-weight atmosphere can produce small spectral features, and high clouds or hazes can obscure deeper atmospheric absorption.
prerequisite_note: A secondary atmosphere is supplied or replenished by processes such as outgassing, rather than simply retained primordial nebular gas.

title: Kepler-452: how much does an Earth-like orbit tell us?
deck: A roughly year-long orbit around a Sun-like star is a starting point for investigation, not a portrait of another Earth.

visual.name: Kepler-452 b
visual.caption: Its appearance and interior are unknown. The disk is schematic, not a picture of a measured surface.

panels: Keep measured properties distinct

Kepler-452 b was identified from repeated transit-like dips around a Sun-like G-type star. NASA’s archive retains it among confirmed planets but flags its detection reliability as controversial. Its radius is about 1.6 Earth radii, its orbital period about 385 days, and its orbital distance about 1.05 AU. These properties motivate comparison with Earth.

A transit primarily constrains a planet’s size relative to its star and its repeating orbital timing. It does not reveal continents, organisms, atmospheric pressure, or a measured ocean. Size alone cannot uniquely determine whether a planet is rocky or volatile-rich.
Consider the star’s history

Kepler-452 is estimated to be older and somewhat more luminous than the Sun. A similar orbital distance therefore need not mean Earth’s present irradiation. Stellar evolution can also move habitable-zone boundaries over time, changing a planet’s environmental history.

Catalog values require provenance. A listed estimated mass should not be treated as an independently measured dynamical mass or used to claim measured density. Atmosphere, surface temperature, water inventory, and interior structure remain unresolved, regardless of the appealing “Earth cousin” nickname.
question: Why would equal orbital distance around two different stars fail to guarantee equal planetary temperature?
answer: Stellar luminosity can differ, and planetary albedo, atmospheric greenhouse effects, heat redistribution, and other conditions also influence temperature.
prerequisite_note: Kepler-452 names the host star; the lowercase b identifies the planet. A G-type star belongs to the same broad spectral class as the Sun, not necessarily the same age or luminosity.

title: LHS 1140: compare possible worlds
deck: Precise mass and radius narrow the possibilities, but they do not uniquely identify an atmosphere or surface ocean.

visual.name: LHS 1140 b
visual.caption: Alternative models, not a measured cross-section. An open substellar ocean is a climate hypothesis only.

panels: Start with independent constraints

LHS 1140 b orbits a red dwarf about every 24.7 days. Its mass is about 5.6 Earth masses and its radius about 1.73 Earth radii. Combining them constrains bulk density, which interior models must reproduce.

Density does not supply a unique composition. Pressure compresses material, and different arrangements of rock, water, and a gaseous envelope can produce similar measurements. Simply comparing the number with Earth’s density can therefore mislead.
Label interpretations honestly

Water-rich interiors and a small light-gas envelope have been considered. Transmission spectra disfavour several tested hydrogen-rich models, while tentative nitrogen-related features remain vulnerable to stellar-contamination uncertainties. Extremely high clouds could hide atmospheric features, but the tested climate models make that explanation less plausible, not impossible.

An “eyeball” illustration with an open ocean facing the star represents a climate scenario. It assumes appropriate atmosphere, water supply, and heat transport. A water-world candidate should not be relabeled as a detected ocean, a confirmed nitrogen atmosphere, or a measured Earth-like surface.
question: Why can a water-rich interpretation remain plausible even when the planet’s mean density is near Earth’s?
answer: Larger rocky planets are more compressed. The expected density must be calculated for the planet’s mass and composition, not inferred solely by comparison with Earth.

title: LHS 1140: follow a disputed helium signal
deck: An evolving atmosphere claim is a chance to practice distinguishing a reported signal from a settled interpretation.

visual.name: LHS 1140 helium timeline
visual.caption: Publication timeline: helium claim July 2026; non-detection analyses August–September 2026. Status as of 23 October 2026.

panels: What was reported?

A July 2026 paper reported helium absorption during a 2024 ground-based transit, but not during a 2025 transit. The authors interpreted the difference as variable escape from a helium-rich upper atmosphere.

That interpretation combines spectral measurements with physical models of atmospheric outflow and stellar irradiation. Even a confirmed upper-atmosphere helium signal would not independently establish the lower atmosphere’s composition, surface pressure, liquid water, or suitability for life.
What did the tests change?

Two independent analyses examined the same four JWST transits and did not find helium at the reported level. None was simultaneous with the positive ground-based observation. A persistent signal is disfavored; an intermittent signal or a spurious original detection remains possible.

The non-detections do not prove that the planet has no atmosphere, and they do not decide whether it is a water world or mini-Neptune. More observations must test the signal and atmosphere without assuming the preferred outcome.
question: Why don’t observations without helium settle what happened on a different date?
answer: The signal could vary with time. The non-detections constrain persistence and strength, but distinguishing variability from a false positive requires further evidence.

title: Where is the liquid?
deck: Always specify the substance, physical state, location, and time before judging whether a water-related clue describes a habitat.

visual.name: Liquid and ice settings
rows: Past water does not establish present life
Ice or vapor is not a liquid habitat
visual.caption: Compare environments rather than assigning invented numerical habitability rankings.

panels: Ask four questions

First ask what substance is present: water, methane, or an acid solution are not interchangeable solvents. Next ask its state: ice, vapor, liquid, and chemically bound water provide different evidence.

Then locate it. Surface lakes and deep isolated reservoirs experience different pressures, temperatures, and chemical supplies. Finally ask when it existed. Ancient minerals and sedimentary landforms can preserve a past wet environment without establishing a modern liquid reservoir.
Connect conditions rather than count ingredients

Habitability depends on conditions working together. Liquid may be physically present but chemically unsuitable, isolated from nutrients, or too short-lived for the process being considered. Heat that maintains liquid is not automatically an accessible metabolic energy source.

Comparisons are strongest when they identify a testable missing connection: Does water touch rock? Can surface chemicals cross the ice? How long did a lake persist? Avoid counting favorable facts as if every ingredient independently added a fixed amount of habitability.
question: A sample contains hydrated minerals. Which conclusion is stronger: past water-rock interaction or a present-day underground ocean?
answer: Past water-rock interaction is supported. Hydrated minerals alone do not establish a present ocean, its size, or its continued existence.

title: The same molecule can tell different stories
deck: A chemical detection becomes meaningful only when its origin, environmental setting, and alternative explanations are considered.

visual.name: Molecules in context
rows: Titan weather; Makemake ice and gas
visual.caption: Examples are chemical comparisons, not a list of confirmed biosignatures.

panels: Separate identification from origin

A reliable spectrum or laboratory measurement can establish that a molecule occurs in sampled material. That is a different claim from explaining how it formed. Biological, geological, atmospheric, and inherited sources can sometimes produce the same molecule.

Even the word “organic” is a chemical description, not a statement that an organism made the material. Amino acids, sugars, and nucleobases are building blocks; detecting them does not demonstrate assembled cells or genetic systems.
Build a stronger argument

Context strengthens interpretation. Ask whether the molecule is associated with particular minerals, a geological setting, a temperature range, or an isotopic pattern. Then test whether nonbiological processes could create the same observations.

Multiple independent clues are more useful than repeating one detection in different words. Contamination controls, measurement uncertainty, preservation, and sampling limitations also matter. A potential biosignature deserves investigation precisely because its biological origin has not yet been established.
question: Why is “organic molecules detected” a weaker claim than “life detected,” even when the measurement is reliable?
answer: Organic compounds can form without biology. Life requires additional evidence of biological origin or organization, evaluated against nonbiological explanations and contamination.

title: Match the evidence to the claim
deck: The best interpretation stays within what the instrument measured and makes each additional assumption visible.

visual.name: Evidence and inference
rows: Induced magnetic response to a changing field
Gas and cloud models, after accounting for the star
visual.caption: Inference is essential to science. The goal is to test assumptions, not to treat all inference as mere guessing.

panels: Trace the reasoning chain

Start with the actual measurement: a brightness, frequency shift, particle count, absorption feature, or laboratory result. State what processing converts it into, then identify the physical model used to interpret it.

A cross-section may summarize the best explanation without being a direct image. The distinction matters when several models fit. Ask what new measurement would separate those alternatives rather than choosing the most vivid illustration.
Understand non-detections

A non-detection constrains a signal at particular sensitivity, wavelengths, locations, and times. It rarely means that the phenomenon is absent everywhere and forever. An atmosphere can have weak features; a plume can vary; an ancient biosignature can fail to survive.

Conversely, a model that fits is not necessarily uniquely required. Strong conclusions emerge when independent evidence converges, alternative explanations fail, and uncertainties are retained. Revision after better data is a strength of the method, not a failure of science.
question: What additional sentence should accompany a claim that an atmospheric gas was not detected?
answer: State the observation’s sensitivity and coverage, plus which concentrations or model scenarios are excluded. Do not silently generalize the result to all atmospheres or times.

title: Transits: measure a missing fraction
deck: A planet crosses its star; a telescope records brightness, not a planetary portrait.
panels: From light curve to size

A transit is a temporary decrease in total stellar brightness when a planet crosses the visible stellar disk. Plot normalized brightness against time. The depth is the missing fraction of light: a fall from 1.000 to 0.990 means a depth of 0.010, or 1%. For a small dark planet making a non-grazing crossing of an approximately uniform, unblended star, depth is approximately the squared planet-to-star radius ratio. Thus a 1% dip implies a radius ratio of 0.10, not 0.01. The interval between consecutive transit centers gives orbital period; the width of one dip gives transit duration.
Geometry filters the discoveries

A planet must pass across the star from our viewing direction, so many real planets never transit. Large planets, small host stars and short periods generally produce easier detections. Repeated dips strengthen the case, but eclipsing stars, blended light and stellar activity must be excluded. Limb darkening, grazing paths and starspots complicate the simple depth formula. Converting radius ratio to planet radius requires the stellar radius. Transit depth alone does not give mass, surface temperature, liquid water or habitability. When comparing two depths around the same star, take a square root before comparing planet sizes.
question: A second planet makes a dip four times deeper around the same star. How do their radii compare?
answer: Its radius is twice as large under the simple transit model, because depth scales as radius squared.

title: Radial velocity: weigh the wobble
deck: The star moves too; spectral-line shifts reveal the component toward or away from us.
panels: From spectrum to velocity

A planet and star orbit their shared center of mass. The star's spectral lines shift toward shorter wavelengths as it approaches and longer wavelengths as it recedes. For speeds much smaller than light speed, radial velocity divided by light speed equals wavelength shift divided by rest wavelength. Plot radial velocity against time after removing the system's overall motion. A simple circular orbit produces an approximately sinusoidal curve. The repeating interval gives period. A curve extending from −20 to +20 meters per second has semi-amplitude K = 20 meters per second; 40 is the full peak-to-peak range. Here the wavelength shift means observed wavelength minus rest wavelength; positive radial velocity means moving away.
Minimum mass, not radius

With stellar mass and an orbital model, the wobble usually constrains planet mass multiplied by sin(i). Here i = 90 degrees is edge-on, while i = 0 is face-on. Unknown inclination therefore leaves a minimum mass: a heavier planet viewed more face-on can produce the same signal. Transits help fix inclination near edge-on, while their depth supplies radius. Massive close-in planets generally create larger signals; long-period planets require long monitoring. Stellar rotation, spots, pulsations and instrumental drift can mimic small Doppler changes. Radial velocity measures line-of-sight motion, not the star's position across the sky.
question: A planet has minimum mass 4 Earth masses and sin(i) = 0.5. What is its actual mass?
answer: Eight Earth masses: divide the minimum mass by sin(i). RV alone supplies no radius.

title: Microlensing: a rare alignment
deck: A foreground system changes the brightness of a background star.
panels: Keep source and lens separate

Gravity bends light. When a foreground lens passes close to our line of sight to a more distant source star, the background star appears temporarily brighter. A planet associated with the foreground lens can introduce a brief perturbation into that brightening pattern. The star being magnified is not the planet's host. Compare the measured brightness-versus-time curve with a single-lens model, then ask whether a planetary model explains the extra feature. The diagram is schematic: surveys generally measure changing combined light rather than resolving separate gravitationally lensed images or watching a planet emit a flash.
Powerful census, difficult revisit

Light-curve modeling can constrain planet-to-host mass ratio and projected separation in lensing units. Absolute planet mass and physical separation require additional information. Event duration alone combines mass, distances and relative transverse motion, so duration is not a unique mass scale. Microlensing can reveal cool, more widely separated planets around faint or distant hosts without detecting planetary light. Dense star fields offer many chances for rare alignments, and rapid observations catch short planetary features. The alignment usually does not repeat, making follow-up difficult. A short isolated event may indicate an unbound planet, but that interpretation requires careful analysis. A planet on a very wide bound orbit can also resemble an isolated lens.
question: Two events last equally long. Must their lens masses be equal?
answer: No. Different distances and relative motions can compensate for different lens masses.

title: Direct imaging: separate faint light
deck: Suppress stellar glare to measure photons from the planet itself.
panels: What an image really provides

Direct imaging separates planetary light from the nearby star. The photons may be reflected starlight or the planet's own thermal emission. Directly imaged exoplanets appear as unresolved points of light, not pictures of continents or clouds. Observations give position relative to the star, brightness in selected bands and sometimes a spectrum. Repeat images can test whether a candidate moves with the star and constrain its orbit. Spectra and colors inform temperature, clouds and composition through models. Brightness is not a unique mass measurement: age, radius, temperature and atmospheric properties all affect how much light a planet emits.
Contrast and separation both matter

A coronagraph suppresses starlight; stable optics, wavefront control and processing reduce remaining glare. Residual speckles can resemble companions, so a faint dot needs verification. A wide orbit around a nearby star is easier to separate angularly than the same orbit farther away. Projected separation in AU divided by distance in parsecs gives angular separation in arcseconds: 10 AU at 20 parsecs is 0.5 arcsecond. Projected separation need not equal orbital semimajor axis. Current infrared imaging favors young, hot giant planets at wide separations. This selection differs strongly from the close-in planets favored by transit surveys.
question: An identical planetary system is placed twice as far away. What happens to angular separation?
answer: It halves. The physical orbit is unchanged, but separating planet light from stellar glare becomes harder.
prerequisite_note: An arcsecond is 1/3,600 degree; a parsec is the distance at which 1 AU spans 1 arcsecond, about 3.26 light-years.

title: Four methods, different missing pieces
deck: Ask what is measured before asking what can be inferred.
panels: Combine complementary constraints

Transit depth yields a size ratio, while radial velocity supplies a mass constraint. For a transiting planet, inclination is near edge-on, reducing the minimum-mass ambiguity. Once mass and radius are available, mean density follows mass divided by volume, so density scales as mass divided by radius cubed.
Worked example: equal mean density

A planet with eight Earth masses and twice Earth's radius has Earth's mean density because 8 divided by 2 cubed equals 1. This does not establish Earth-like geology: different combinations of core, mantle, water and gas can share a mean density.
Correct for what each survey misses

A catalog is not an unbiased inventory of all planets. Transit surveys require alignment and favor repeated, deeper dips. RV favors stronger stellar wobbles and sufficiently quiet stars. Microlensing depends on rare geometry but accesses populations difficult to study through host-star light. Imaging favors favorable contrast and wide angular separation. Population claims require corrections for sensitivity and selection. Agreement between independent methods strengthens interpretation, but no single detection method demonstrates habitability or life. Atmospheres need further observations, and atmospheric interpretation still requires stellar, climate and chemical context. A non-detection must always be tied to an instrument's sensitivity.
question: Why does equal mean density not prove two planets have identical interiors?
answer: Density is one bulk quantity. Different layer compositions and proportions can produce the same mass-to-volume ratio.

title: Design the platform around the question
deck: Power, environment and communications determine which measurements are practical.
panels: Environment sets the design

A scientific objective becomes a spacecraft requirement. At five times Earth's distance from the Sun, sunlight provides only one twenty-fifth of the flux, so solar-powered missions need large arrays and careful energy budgets. Radioisotope systems provide power without depending directly on illumination, but power remains finite. Venus descent probes face intense heat and pressure; Jupiter missions face radiation; infrared telescopes need cold optics and detectors. Shielding, thermal control and redundancy add mass. Launch capacity, fuel and gravity assists constrain trajectories. There is no universally best design: each choice purchases scientific capability at a cost.
Time, data and autonomy

An orbiter can revisit a region, whereas a descent probe obtains a detailed profile along one path. A flyby provides a short close-up window but may avoid prolonged radiation exposure. A rover connects measurements to particular rocks, yet covers little terrain. Communications distance limits data return and makes real-time driving impossible. Missions prioritize observations, compress data and use autonomous fault protection. Higher image resolution usually increases data volume or reduces coverage. Sample return adds collection, reentry and contamination-control demands but enables powerful Earth laboratory work. Explain an engineering choice by linking it to the measurement it preserves.
question: Why can a brief probe descent answer a question that a long-lived orbiter cannot answer as directly?
answer: The probe samples local atmospheric gases and conditions in place, while the orbiter generally infers them remotely over broader areas.

title: An instrument measures a signal
deck: Learn the chain: physical signal → instrument → inference → alternative explanation.
panels: Different kinds of composition

A camera records spatial brightness, revealing landforms, textures and changes. A light spectrometer measures intensity versus wavelength; comparison with laboratory spectra constrains molecules or minerals, but mixtures, clouds and temperature can complicate identification. A mass spectrometer analyzes particles entering the instrument through their mass-to-charge behavior. It samples a local gas or delivered material, not an entire planet. Instruments must be calibrated, and contamination controls matter when interpreting small chemical signals. Knowing that an instrument measures organics is incomplete: ask where the material came from, what preparation occurred, and which alternative compounds or processes fit the measurement.
Interiors require indirect reasoning

Radar sends radio waves and measures returning echoes. Delay constrains distance or inferred depth, while echo strength depends on material properties and geometry. A bright reflector does not automatically mean liquid water. Magnetometers measure fields: a changing external field can induce a response in a conducting layer, consistent with a salty ocean. Plasma effects and different interior structures can complicate the interpretation. Radio tracking measures spacecraft motion; gravity models then constrain internal mass distribution and tidal deformation. Combining independent measurements can reject alternatives that fit one instrument alone. None of these instruments is a universal life detector.
question: Why pair a magnetometer with plasma measurements when investigating an icy moon?
answer: Plasma can alter the measured magnetic field; measuring it helps separate environmental effects from an ocean-induced response.

title: Venus: observe, then descend
deck: Venus Express is completed; DAVINCI is in development. Status: 23 October 2026.

visual.headline: Two ways to read an atmosphere

panels: Venus Express: a changing atmosphere

Venus Express studied atmospheric circulation, chemistry and escape from orbit. VIRTIS measured visible/infrared radiance, while SPICAV/SOIR spectra and occultations constrained gases and vertical structure. Cloud images tracked motion; ASPERA-4 sampled particles associated with solar-wind interactions and atmospheric escape. Magnetic and radio measurements supplied additional environmental context. Repeated orbital observations revealed variation over time without exposing a spacecraft to Venus's surface conditions. The limitation is important: remotely inferred composition is not the same as directly sampling every atmospheric layer. Different viewing geometries, wavelengths and instruments were needed to separate overlapping atmospheric effects.
DAVINCI: atmospheric history in place

DAVINCI will combine a flyby carrier with an atmospheric descent probe. VMS and VTLS will measure gases and isotopic information, including clues to volatile origins and water history. VASI will measure pressure, temperature and winds; VenDI will image Alpha Regio during descent. VfOx targets oxygen chemistry, not breathable air. Carrier instruments add cloud and surface context. A heat shield, pressure vessel and relay protect and recover the brief descent record. Precision along one path comes at the cost of narrow coverage. These are planned measurements, not evidence already returned or a promise of a long-lived surface lander.
question: Why do gas isotopes and cloud-motion images answer different questions?
answer: Isotopes constrain origin and evolution; cloud motion constrains present circulation. Both inform Venus's history but measure different physical properties.

title: VERITAS: read the surface through clouds
deck: Future Venus orbiter in development. Status: 23 October 2026.
panels: What the instruments will test

VERITAS will investigate how Venus's surface and interior evolved and whether volcanism and deformation remain active. VISAR will use synthetic-aperture radar for surface mapping and interferometric measurements for topography and change. Radio waves can reach the ground through clouds that block ordinary visible views. VEM will measure near-infrared emission through atmospheric windows to constrain surface emissivity, rock properties and volcanic activity. Tracking the spacecraft's motion will constrain the gravity field. These observations connect landforms, surface materials and internal structure, rather than assuming one image reveals the entire history of the planet.
Why repeat the measurement?

A single map describes appearance; comparable maps made at different times can test change. Detecting subtle deformation requires controlled viewing geometry and careful processing, not simply subtracting arbitrary pictures. Radar brightness depends on roughness, material properties and orientation, so it is not an ordinary color photograph or a complete view through rock. Infrared composition and gravity interpretations also depend on models. VERITAS complements Venus Express's atmospheric record and DAVINCI's planned descent profile: global geological coverage, repeated atmospheric observations and direct local chemistry address different parts of the climate–surface–interior system. Large data volumes make processing and communications part of the science design.
question: What extra question can repeated radar observations address beyond a single geological map?
answer: Whether surface position or appearance changes over time, potentially indicating deformation or activity, after instrumental and viewing differences are controlled.

title: Mars: connect orbit to a rock
deck: Perseverance and MRO are active; MRO’s CRISM is retired. Status: 23 October 2026.
panels: MRO: choose and understand a region

Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter links detailed observations to broad context. HiRISE resolves small landforms and hazards; CTX places them within regional geology. Archived CRISM spectra identify minerals associated with water-related alteration, although CRISM stopped operating in 2023. SHARAD radar echoes constrain subsurface layers and buried ice, with material properties and surface clutter complicating interpretation. MARCI and MCS follow atmospheric weather and structure. MRO also relays communications. Fine resolution does not mean direct chemical sampling, and a radargram is echo delay along a track, not a photograph of an exposed underground wall.
Perseverance: inspect the geological setting

Perseverance investigates ancient habitability and possible biosignatures while caching documented samples. Mastcam-Z supplies imaging context; SuperCam examines remote chemistry; PIXL maps elemental composition; SHERLOC probes minerals and organic compounds with spectroscopy. RIMFAX investigates shallow layering and MEDA measures weather. MOXIE demonstrated oxygen production from atmospheric carbon dioxide, then concluded its experiment in 2023. It was not a life detector. A rover links chemistry to rock texture but covers little of Mars. Cached tubes have not thereby reached Earth. Organic compounds require contamination checks and tests of nonbiological origins before supporting claims about ancient life.
question: Why is a water-related mineral map valuable before a rover studies individual rocks?
answer: It identifies promising regions and geological context; the rover can then test specific materials and textures that remote spectra cannot fully resolve.

title: MAVEN: reconstruct atmospheric loss
deck: Completed: NASA declared the mission ended 3 June 2026. Status checked 23 October 2026.

visual.headline: From particle escape to climate history

panels: The atmosphere meets space

MAVEN investigated how Mars loses atmospheric material and how that loss responds to the Sun. NGIMS measured neutral and ion composition and isotopes; IUVS examined ultraviolet signals from the upper atmosphere. SWIA, SWEA and SEP characterized incoming solar-wind and energetic particles. STATIC measured ion populations, while MAG and LPW measured magnetic and plasma conditions. Its elliptical orbit sampled different regions of the upper atmosphere and surrounding space. Correlating solar inputs with atmospheric responses connected a physical mechanism to a measured loss process. These are historical mission results, not measurements from a currently operating orbiter.
From present processes to the past

Atmospheric escape helps explain how Mars changed from earlier environments capable of sustaining surface water to the present thin atmosphere. However, multiplying one modern loss rate by billions of years is not a reliable reconstruction: the young Sun, atmosphere and planetary conditions differed. Isotopes and physical models help connect measured processes to long-term evolution. MAVEN complements rather than replaces surface evidence. MRO maps minerals and landscapes; Perseverance examines local rock records; MAVEN studied a mechanism of atmospheric transformation. Loss of contact occurred in December 2025, and NASA ended the mission in June 2026 after recovery efforts.
question: Why is “today’s escape rate × Mars’s age” an inadequate estimate of total atmospheric loss?
answer: Solar forcing, atmospheric composition and escape conditions evolved; the rate was not necessarily constant through time.

title: Europa: build an ocean argument
deck: Galileo is completed; Europa Clipper is cruising to Jupiter. Status: 23 October 2026.
panels: Galileo: converging lines of evidence

Galileo's images revealed icy-moon geology, while NIMS measured near-infrared composition. Magnetic measurements supported electrically conducting subsurface layers, plausibly salty liquid water. This was an interior inference, not an ocean photograph or biological detection. Plasma measurements helped interpret the magnetic environment. The mission also carried a separate probe into Jupiter's atmosphere. Radioisotope power supported operations far from the Sun. When its high-gain antenna failed to deploy, compression, low-gain communications and improved ground reception preserved valuable science. Its deliberate final plunge into Jupiter reduced the chance of contaminating Europa in the future.
Clipper: test habitability, not life

Europa Clipper will orbit Jupiter and repeatedly fly by Europa, limiting time in intense radiation. EIS images and E-THEMIS thermal measurements will map geology and temperatures; MISE will constrain surface composition. REASON radar will probe ice structure, while ECM and PIMS jointly examine magnetic and plasma effects. MASPEX samples gases and SUDA analyzes dust grains; Europa-UVS studies ultraviolet signals. Radio tracking adds gravity constraints. Multiple instruments can reject competing interior explanations. Clipper carries no lander, does not guarantee a plume encounter and will not prove life exists. Its Europa investigations are still ahead during cruise.
question: Why is a magnetic response consistent with an ocean stronger when combined with geological and gravity evidence?
answer: Independent measurements test different properties and help exclude alternative explanations that could fit the magnetic signal alone.

title: JUICE: compare the ocean moons
deck: ESA’s mission is cruising toward Jupiter. Status: 23 October 2026.

visual.headline: System comparison, then Ganymede
labels: Fields, radar and tides work together

panels: Measure more than one property

JUICE will investigate Jupiter's environment and the icy moons Ganymede, Callisto and Europa, eventually orbiting Ganymede. JANUS images and MAJIS spectra will link geology to surface composition. GALA laser ranging will measure topography and tidal deformation; RIME radar will probe structure within ice. J-MAG measurements, interpreted with particle and plasma observations from PEP and RPWI, will constrain magnetic environments and interiors. The 3GM radio investigation will constrain gravity and related structure. UVS and SWI will study atmospheric and exospheric properties. No single measurement guarantees a complete map of an ocean or its underlying rock.
Why Ganymede orbit changes the science

Flybys permit comparisons among worlds, but each close encounter has a brief measurement window. Orbiting Ganymede will enable repeated, focused observations that improve spatial coverage and tests of change. Europa Clipper instead concentrates repeated Jupiter-orbit flybys on Europa. Together, their approaches examine whether different icy environments share habitability-relevant processes. Large solar arrays address weak sunlight; shielding, thermal control and fault protection address a harsh environment. Precise tracking and multiple instruments help separate uncertain ocean depth, salinity and layer thickness. JUICE's planned measurements must be described as future tests, not discoveries already returned during cruise.
question: What does sustained Ganymede orbit offer that a single flyby cannot?
answer: Repeated observations improve coverage and allow measurements of variation, while a flyby provides only a brief local encounter.

title: Cassini–Huygens: two viewpoints
deck: Completed mission: Saturn orbiter plus Titan descent probe. Status: 23 October 2026.

visual.headline: Repeated flybys meet one landing
labels: Huygens measured one descent and site

panels: Cassini: remote maps and local samples

Cassini orbited Saturn, repeatedly observing moons, rings and the atmosphere. Its RADAR mapped Titan's surface through haze, revealing landforms such as lakes, channels and dunes. Cameras and ultraviolet, infrared and thermal spectra added shape, composition and temperature. At Enceladus, INMS measured gases while CDA analyzed dust and ice grains, connecting plume chemistry to inferred ocean processes. Field, particle and gravity measurements added independent context. A plume sample does not represent every location or depth of an ocean. Salts, organics and chemical-energy clues support habitability arguments but do not establish organisms.
Huygens: ground truth beneath the haze

Huygens descended through Titan's atmosphere and landed at one site; Cassini itself did not land there. GCMS analyzed atmospheric chemistry, HASI measured physical and electrical properties, and DISR supplied descent images and spectra. Radio measurements constrained winds, and surface instruments tested local physical properties. Huygens traded broad coverage for direct measurements along one path, relying on stored power and a relay link. Cassini's radioisotope power supported a long orbital investigation in weak sunlight. Its controlled final entry into Saturn protected potentially habitable moons from accidental contamination. Global context and local measurements answered complementary questions.
question: Why can Huygens’s direct measurements not substitute for Cassini’s repeated orbital observations?
answer: One descent and landing describe a limited place and time; repeated orbital measurements provide regional, global and seasonal context.

title: Dragonfly: follow Titan’s chemistry
deck: Future rotorcraft lander in development. Status: 23 October 2026.

visual.headline: Move between chemical settings
labels: Drill and transfer a surface sample

panels: From collected material to an explanation

Dragonfly will investigate Titan's organic chemistry by visiting multiple surface settings. DrACO will drill and transfer samples; DraMS will analyze chemical composition by mass spectrometry. These have different jobs: collection hardware does not itself identify molecules. DraGNS will measure elemental composition, DragonCam will record geological context, and DraGMet will investigate local environmental and geophysical conditions. Comparing chemistry across different landscapes can test how ingredients and processing environments interact. Titan's carbon-rich chemistry is not equivalent to biology, and its surface methane/ethane liquids must not be confused with ordinary liquid-water habitats.
Why fly rather than drive?

Titan's dense atmosphere and low gravity make rotorcraft flight useful for crossing terrain difficult for wheels. Multiple landings allow sampling of separated sites rather than extrapolating from one location. That mobility requires navigation, hazard assessment and repeated safe landings. Weak sunlight favors an MMRTG that steadily charges a battery for higher-power activities such as flight. Communication delays rule out joystick piloting from Earth, so autonomy is central to the design. Huygens supplied a single descent and landing record; Dragonfly is designed for repeated local investigations. No Titan flight or sample measurements have yet been returned by this future mission.
question: Why does Dragonfly need both a steady power source and a rechargeable battery?
answer: The source supplies sustained energy; the battery stores it for operations whose peak power demand exceeds that steady output.

title: OSIRIS-REx: bring the evidence home
deck: Bennu sample return is completed; laboratory research continues. Status: 23 October 2026.

visual.headline: Reconnaissance → collection → laboratory
labels: TAGSAM collects; it does not analyze

panels: Know the sample’s original setting

OSIRIS-REx mapped Bennu before touching its surface. OCAMS images documented terrain and boulders; OLA laser ranging constrained three-dimensional shape. OVIRS and OTES measured reflected and thermal spectra to investigate composition, temperature and mineral properties. TAGSAM then collected material using a nitrogen-gas-assisted touch-and-go operation. It was a sampling device, not a spectrometer. Reconnaissance connected the chosen site to the asteroid's broader geological setting and helped navigate its weak gravity and hazardous surface. The returned material can test water-related alteration and the chemistry of primitive Solar System ingredients without claiming that every part of Bennu was sampled.
Why return instead of analyze only there?

Earth laboratories can apply sensitive, repeated and future techniques that cannot all fit on a spacecraft. That advantage demands precise collection, return, recovery and curation. Terrestrial moisture, oxygen and organic contamination could confuse interpretations, so sample history and clean controls are essential evidence. Organic molecules or amino acids demonstrate chemistry, not asteroid life. A small surface collection also cannot represent every depth or region. The Bennu sample-return phase is complete, while sample studies continue; the spacecraft moved into a renamed mission. Do not confuse completed delivery with completed scientific interpretation: new laboratory questions can be asked for years.
question: Why is contamination control part of the scientific argument rather than merely housekeeping?
answer: Without it, a detected compound might come from Earth or handling rather than Bennu, undermining the inference about asteroid chemistry.

title: Rosetta: watch a comet change
deck: Completed rendezvous mission at 67P with the Philae lander. Status: 23 October 2026.

visual.headline: A time series, not a snapshot
labels: Images track jets and surface change
Gas and dust carry chemical information
Solar heating changes the sampled material

panels: Follow activity through changing sunlight

Rosetta accompanied comet 67P rather than making only a brief flyby. OSIRIS images tracked nucleus shape, jets and changes. ROSINA measured gas composition and isotopes; COSIMA examined dust composition, while GIADA and MIDAS constrained grain properties and structure. Infrared, ultraviolet and microwave observations added composition, temperature and outgassing information. Observing through changing solar heating connected processes to activity over time. However, the coma is material released from the nucleus, not an unbiased inventory of every buried layer. Different species and grains can be released or transported differently, so sample location and timing matter.
Landing and power are coupled

Philae was designed to add direct surface measurements and work with Rosetta on radio sounding. Its anchoring system failed, and it bounced into a shaded location that limited solar recharge. Instrument design goals must not be mistaken for a claim that every intended drilling or sample analysis succeeded. Rosetta's large solar arrays and earlier hibernation addressed power constraints during a long journey. Compared with OSIRIS-REx, Rosetta emphasized in-place time evolution rather than returning samples to Earth. Both missions connect primitive materials to Solar System history; neither shows that the presence of life's ingredients necessarily produced life.
question: What scientific advantage did rendezvous provide over a fast flyby of 67P?
answer: It allowed repeated measurements as solar heating and activity changed, helping link observations to evolving comet processes.

title: Kepler finds; Webb characterizes
deck: Kepler is retired; JWST is active. Status: 23 October 2026.
panels: Kepler: count planets with a geometry filter

Kepler's CCD photometer measured stellar brightness repeatedly, identifying periodic dips that constrain orbital period and planet-to-star radius ratio. Stable pointing and calibration were essential for detecting small changes. The original survey stared at one field; K2 used an adapted pointing strategy after reaction-wheel failures. Operations ended in 2018, but archived data remain scientifically useful. A detected sample is not the full population: occurrence estimates must correct for orbital alignment, sensitivity and observing duration. Longer-period planets produce fewer transits in a fixed survey. Kepler did not resolve planetary continents or establish atmospheric habitability.
JWST: analyze selected planetary light

JWST's NIRCam, NIRSpec, NIRISS and MIRI provide infrared imaging and spectroscopic capabilities. Wavelength-dependent transits, eclipses and phase changes constrain gases, clouds, temperature and heat transport; some planets can also be imaged directly. A sunshield keeps the observatory cold, and MIRI receives additional cryocooling to reduce the telescope's own infrared interference. Atmospheric retrievals depend on models and calibration. A weak spectral feature might reflect clouds, low abundance or limited sensitivity rather than universal absence. Stellar variability can contaminate a planetary signal. One molecule, even confidently identified, is not automatically evidence of biology.
question: Why does Kepler’s discovery of a planet not guarantee that JWST can determine its atmospheric composition?
answer: Atmospheric signals may be too faint, obscured by clouds or contaminated by stellar effects; discovery and characterization have different requirements.

title: Roman: extend the planetary census
deck: Launched 30 August 2026; commissioning update as of 13 November 2026.

visual.headline: Two instruments, different purposes
labels: Wide Field Instrument: survey light curves

panels: A wide field catches rare events

Roman's Wide Field Instrument is an infrared survey camera with spectroscopic capability. Repeated observations of dense Galactic-bulge fields will monitor changing stellar brightness, including microlensing events and transits. Observing many stars simultaneously increases opportunities to catch rare alignments; rapid revisits help capture brief planetary perturbations. Microlensing complements transit surveys by probing cool, more widely separated planets and potentially unbound objects. Individual systems are often distant and difficult to characterize afterward. Roman therefore expands the statistical census rather than guaranteeing detailed atmospheric analysis of each discovered planet. Survey interpretation still requires selection and sensitivity corrections.
A technology demonstration is not a promise

Roman's Coronagraph Instrument tests suppression of stellar glare for high-contrast observations of faint planets and disks. Stable optics and wavefront control are essential because residual starlight can overwhelm a companion. This role differs from the Wide Field Instrument's survey work and is not a promise to image Earth twins or detect life. Roman launched on 30 August 2026. In its 13 November 2026 update, NASA reported precise instrument alignment, with further coronagraph tests ahead as commissioning continued toward science operations. Planned survey discoveries are not completed results. Compare the observatories: Kepler supplies a transit census, JWST examines selected targets, and Roman adds complementary survey reach and imaging technology.
question: Why should Roman’s coronagraph goals not be described as guaranteed Earth-like planet discoveries?
answer: It is a technology demonstration with contrast, stability and target limitations, not a completed or guaranteed Earth-twin census.

title: How shifted light reveals motion
deck: Use a line’s displacement relative to its laboratory wavelength.

visual.meaning: Low-speed Doppler shift • radial velocity only

panels: Define the quantities

The wavelength change is Δλ = λobserved − λ₀, where λ₀ is the rest wavelength. The approximate relation applies when the radial speed is much smaller than the speed of light c. A positive radial velocity means recession in this convention. Motion across the sky does not produce this first-order radial signal.
Worked proportion

Suppose the fractional shift is 10⁻⁴. With c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the radial speed is 3 × 10⁴ m/s, or 30 km/s. If the shift doubles for the same line, the inferred speed doubles. For a planet search, repeated tiny changes in the star’s line position reveal orbital motion; the star’s constant systemic velocity is not itself evidence of a planet.
question: A line at 600 nm shifts by +0.06 nm. Find Δλ/λ₀ and explain the direction of motion.
answer: 0.06/600 = 10⁻⁴. The positive wavelength shift is a redshift, corresponding to recession; vᵣ ≈ 30 km/s.

title: Distance spreads the same light
deck: Luminosity is total power; flux is power arriving per unit area.
panels: Derive the inverse square

An isotropic star’s luminosity L spreads over a sphere of area 4πr². Thus flux F = L/(4πr²), in watts per square meter. The light is not being “used up” in empty space: the same power is shared over a larger area. Absorption along the path would be an additional effect, not part of this simple relationship.
Worked comparison

At twice the distance from the same star, flux falls to one quarter. At three times the distance, it falls to one ninth. For two different stars, F₂/F₁ = (L₂/L₁)(r₁/r₂)². A planet around a star four times as luminous receives the same flux at twice the orbital distance. Use ratios before inserting numbers; most factors cancel.
question: A star has 9 times the Sun’s luminosity. At what distance in AU would its planet receive Earth’s incident flux?
answer: 3 AU: 9/3² = 1. This compares incoming flux, not surface temperatures.

title: Albedo: reflected versus absorbed
deck: For an energy budget, use Bond albedo: the total reflected fraction.
panels: Keep the areas straight

A sphere intercepts a parallel beam across its projected disk, πR², not its entire surface area. Bond albedo A is dimensionless and lies between zero and one. It integrates reflection over wavelengths and directions. A geometric albedo describes a different brightness comparison and should not be substituted silently into a global energy calculation.
Worked energy accounting

If A = 0.25, a quarter of incoming power is reflected and three quarters is absorbed. If albedo rises to 0.50 at fixed flux and radius, absorbed power changes by 0.50/0.75 = 2/3. Temperature does not fall by the same fraction, because thermal emission depends on the fourth power of absolute temperature. A bright cloud deck can also participate in greenhouse processes, so reflection alone does not determine surface conditions.
question: Two equal-sized planets receive equal flux. Their albedos are 0.2 and 0.6. Which absorbs twice as much power?
answer: The A = 0.2 planet absorbs 0.8 of incident power; the A = 0.6 planet absorbs 0.4. The first absorbs twice as much.

title: Hotter surfaces radiate much more
deck: Stefan–Boltzmann relates total thermal emission to absolute temperature.

visual.caption: Idealized fixed-emissivity relationship; axes have no numerical scale.

panels: A fourth-power relationship

The emitted power per unit area is Femit = εσT⁴. Here σ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and ε is emissivity; an ideal blackbody has ε = 1. Total emitted power also includes emitting area. Use kelvin, never Celsius, in a temperature power. An object at 0°C is about 273 K and certainly emits thermal radiation.
Worked scaling

At fixed area and emissivity, doubling T increases emitted power by 2⁴ = 16. Conversely, increasing the required radiated power by a factor of 16 raises equilibrium T by a factor of two. A factor of four in power raises T only by √2. This weak fourth-root response is why large changes in stellar input produce smaller fractional changes in simple radiative temperature.
question: A surface radiates 81 times as much power per square meter at unchanged emissivity. How has its Kelvin temperature changed?
answer: It has tripled, because 3⁴ = 81. This is a Kelvin ratio, not a Celsius ratio.

title: A hotter spectrum peaks bluer
deck: Wien’s law uses the peak of the spectrum expressed per unit wavelength.
panels: Read both height and location

For a blackbody, λmax T = b, where b ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. Increasing temperature shifts the wavelength peak toward shorter wavelengths while increasing total emission. A plotted spectrum per unit frequency has a different peak definition: do not switch between frequency and wavelength plots using a simple reciprocal of the peak.
Worked estimate

A 300 K body peaks near 10 micrometers: 3 × 10⁻³ divided by 3 × 10² gives 10⁻⁵ meters. A 6000 K star peaks near 0.5 micrometers. These order-of-magnitude estimates explain why relatively cool worlds emit strongly in infrared light while a Sun-like star emits strongly in visible light. Real atmospheres and surfaces add absorption features and depart from perfect blackbodies.
question: Two approximate blackbodies peak at 5 μm and 10 μm. Which is hotter, and by what factor?
answer: The 5 μm source is twice as hot. Peak wavelength and absolute temperature are inversely proportional.

title: Build an equilibrium temperature
deck: Balance absorbed starlight against thermal radiation to space.
panels: Derive rather than memorize

For a uniformly radiating spherical planet, absorbed power is (1 − A)FπR² and emitted power is 4πR²εσT⁴. Set them equal and cancel πR²: T = [(1 − A)F/(4εσ)]¹/⁴. The four comes from emitting-sphere area divided by intercepting-disk area. The model assumes global redistribution, no internal heating, and a simple gray emissivity.
What this temperature is not

This effective equilibrium benchmark is not necessarily the surface temperature. Atmospheres can redistribute heat and alter the altitude from which radiation escapes. For fixed albedo and emissivity, T ∝ L¹/⁴r⁻¹/². Moving four times farther from the same star halves T. Changing the assumptions about day-night redistribution changes the geometric factor; state your model before comparing answers.
question: A planet moves from r to 4r with no changes in albedo or emissivity. What happens to flux and equilibrium temperature?
answer: Flux becomes 1/16 as large; equilibrium temperature becomes (1/16)¹/⁴ = 1/2 as large in kelvin.

title: Energy connects motion and gravity
deck: Choose and state the zero of potential energy before using its sign.

visual.meaning: Gravitational potential energy is zero at infinity.

panels: Interpret the signs

Kinetic energy K measures motion and is nonnegative. For two isolated gravitating bodies, U = −GMm/r when zero is assigned at infinite separation. Moving outward makes U less negative, so gravitational potential energy increases. The familiar mgh formula is a near-surface approximation for a small height change where g is nearly constant, not a replacement for the general expression across a planetary system.
Work an energy comparison

At fixed mass, doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy. At twice the center-to-center distance, gravitational potential energy has half its former negative magnitude. In an ideal unpowered orbit, total mechanical energy stays constant while K and U exchange. Drag, thrust and tidal dissipation change this simple accounting and must be included when relevant.
question: A spacecraft climbs outward without thrust or drag. As its potential energy increases, what must happen to its kinetic energy?
answer: Its kinetic energy decreases by the same amount in the ideal isolated model, conserving K + U.

title: Gravity: mass and separation
deck: The separation in Newton’s law is measured between centers of mass.

visual.meaning: Force on a test mass m versus acceleration at distance r

panels: Separate force from acceleration

The force between two masses is proportional to both masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. Divide by the small body’s mass m to obtain its acceleration. Ideal freely falling objects at the same position therefore have the same gravitational acceleration regardless of their masses. A planet’s surface g uses r equal to its radius, not its orbital distance from the star.
Use units to check reasoning

G has units m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻². Multiplying by mass and dividing by distance squared leaves m s⁻², the units of acceleration. If a proposed formula produces meters per second instead, it describes a speed or is wrong. For a planet with twice Earth’s mass and twice Earth’s radius, surface gravity is 2/2² = 1/2 of Earth’s, despite the larger mass.
question: At three times a planet’s radius from its center, how large is its gravity compared with the surface value?
answer: One ninth, assuming the same spherical central body and no other significant forces.

title: Orbits obey three connected laws
deck: For a small planet orbiting the same central star, P² is proportional to a³.
panels: Geometry and changing speed

Kepler’s first law describes an ellipse with the central body at a focus, not generally at the center. The second law says the line joining the orbiting body to the central body sweeps equal areas in equal times. The planet therefore moves faster near periapsis and slower near apoapsis. These laws describe ideal two-body motion; real systems can have perturbations.
Period from orbital size

The general relation is P² = 4π²a³/[G(M + m)]. For planets much less massive than the same star, the denominator is effectively constant. If semimajor axis a grows by a factor of four, period P grows by √(4³) = 8. Do not use instantaneous star-planet distance in place of semimajor axis for an eccentric orbit. Across different stellar masses, include the mass factor.
question: A planet around the same star has a period 27 times longer. What is its semimajor-axis ratio?
answer: 9: if a grows by 9, P grows by √(9³) = 27.

title: Escape speed comes from energy
deck: Minimum escape speed is the threshold for reaching infinity with zero remaining speed in the ideal model.

visual.meaning: Set ½mv² − GMm/r = 0; cancel m and solve.

panels: Derive the threshold

At the threshold of escape, total mechanical energy is zero when gravitational potential is zero at infinity. Solving ½mv² = GMm/r gives escape speed. The escaping object’s mass cancels. This ideal expression neglects atmosphere, rotation, thrust after launch and other gravitating bodies. Being in orbit does not mean escaping: a circular orbit at radius r has the smaller speed √(GM/r).
Connect to atmospheric retention

Compare the gravitational threshold with a distribution of molecular speeds rather than one speed for every particle. Thermal speed scales roughly as √(T/molecule mass). Heating gas or lowering molecular mass increases typical speed. This explains a tendency for hot, weak-gravity worlds to lose light gases, but ultraviolet heating and nonthermal escape also matter; the simple comparison is not a complete atmospheric model.
question: A planet has 4 times the mass and the same radius as another. How do their escape speeds compare?
answer: The more massive planet has twice the escape speed: √4 = 2.

title: Tides fall off faster than gravity
deck: A tide measures the change in gravitational pull across an extended body.
panels: Compare two distance laws

The gravitational acceleration scale is GM/r². Across a small moon of radius R, the near-far change scales as GMR/r³, up to geometry-dependent factors. Thus doubling separation reduces the tidal acceleration scale by about eight, not four. The approximation assumes R is much smaller than r. Strong gravity and strong differential gravity are related but not identical ideas.
Do not confuse force with heating

Tidal heating requires changing deformation and dissipation, not merely a static stretch. Eccentricity, orbital frequency, material rigidity and internal friction matter. Resonances can maintain eccentricity, allowing continuing dissipation. The r⁻³ acceleration rule is not a universal formula for tidal heating power. Europa and Enceladus connect this mechanics to subsurface liquid and potentially useful water-rock chemistry.
question: At unchanged masses and size, separation triples. What happens to the tidal acceleration scale? Does that alone specify the heat output?
answer: The tidal acceleration scale falls to 1/27. No: heating also depends on changing deformation, orbit and material properties.

title: Gas: pressure, volume, temperature
deck: Use absolute temperature and distinguish amount from density.

visual.meaning: n: moles; N: particles; R = N_A k_B

panels: What the idealization assumes

An ideal gas treats particles as having negligible volume and neglects intermolecular interactions except during collisions. It is useful for many dilute gases, but can fail near condensation or at high density. Pressure is force per unit area; temperature describes the energy scale of random motion. The same temperature does not give every molecule the same speed, nor the same speed distribution for different molecular masses.
State what stays fixed

For a sealed rigid container, n and V are fixed, so doubling Kelvin temperature doubles pressure. At fixed temperature and gas amount, doubling volume halves pressure. For a fixed-composition ideal gas, density is proportional to P/T. Heating from 20°C to 40°C is not a doubling of temperature: compare about 293 K with 313 K instead.
question: A sealed rigid gas sample cools from 400 K to 300 K. What is its new pressure relative to its initial pressure?
answer: It is 300/400 = 3/4 of its initial pressure, assuming ideal-gas behavior and no loss or condensation.

title: Reaction rates face energy barriers
deck: Arrhenius describes how temperature changes a rate constant in a common model.

visual.caption: ln k = ln A − Eₐ/(RT); slope = −Eₐ/R for a simple Arrhenius model.

panels: Read the exponential

The Arrhenius equation is k = A exp[−Eₐ/(RT)], where k is a rate constant, A a prefactor and Eₐ an activation energy per mole. At fixed A and positive Eₐ, higher T makes the exponent less negative and increases k. This is not a fourth-power or inverse-square relationship. The units of k depend on the reaction’s rate law; do not automatically assign seconds⁻¹.
Connect rate to habitability

Warmth may accelerate useful reactions, but also destabilize molecules or membranes. A catalyst offers a lower-barrier pathway and accelerates approach to equilibrium; it does not change the equilibrium position at a given temperature. On a graph of ln k against 1/T, a more negative slope corresponds to a larger activation energy. Be careful: moving right on that graph means lower, not higher, temperature.
question: On a plot of ln k versus 1/T, why does a negative slope still mean the reaction gets faster as temperature increases?
answer: Increasing T decreases 1/T, so you move left on the horizontal axis, where ln k is larger.

title: Equilibrium is dynamic, not frozen
deck: Reaction direction, reaction speed and continued supply are different questions.
panels: Separate composition from rate

At chemical equilibrium, forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates, so bulk composition no longer changes. Reactant and product concentrations need not be equal. A reaction quotient Q describes the current mixture; comparing Q with the equilibrium constant K indicates the favored direction under the stated conditions. For a written reaction, Q < K favors net forward change; Q > K favors reverse change.
Keep an energy source renewed

A system away from equilibrium can offer usable chemical energy. If no process resupplies reactants, reactions tend to reduce the available imbalance. Geological flow, sunlight or transport can maintain disequilibrium. Whether a reaction is favorable is distinct from whether it occurs quickly: an activation barrier may make it slow. This distinction is central to interpreting potential biosignatures and the chemistry around hydrothermal environments.
question: Does a catalyst make an unfavorable equilibrium mixture favorable, or mainly change how quickly equilibrium is approached?
answer: It changes kinetics by providing another pathway; it does not change the equilibrium constant or equilibrium composition at the same temperature.

title: A toolkit for unfamiliar problems
deck: Write the relationship, cancel common factors, and check the units.

items: Ratio first: compare two states before substituting numbers.
Rearrange: isolate the quantity the question actually asks for.
Units: carry meters, seconds, kilograms and kelvin.
Estimate: powers of ten reveal implausible answers.

panels: A reusable solution sequence

First list what changes and what is held fixed. Write a symbolic relationship and form a ratio between the two cases. Cancel identical constants. Apply powers to the ratios, not to isolated numbers without units. Then explain the result in words. An answer such as “one quarter” is incomplete unless it names the quantity: flux, temperature, force or some other variable.
Estimate before calculating

For multiplication, combine leading factors and add powers of ten. For division, divide factors and subtract exponents. A kilometer is 10³ meters; a micrometer is 10⁻⁶ meters. Areas square the conversion and volumes cube it. Check limiting cases: increasing distance should not increase inverse-square flux. If a problem supplies a graph, read axis scale, units, uncertainty and whether it is linear or logarithmic before interpreting a trend.
question: Convert 2 km² into m², then explain why multiplying by only 1000 would be wrong.
answer: 2 km² = 2 × (10³ m)² = 2 × 10⁶ m². Both length dimensions must be converted.

chapter: Put the clues together: integrated reasoning
title: Read the whole evidence chain
deck: Separate what was measured from what remains uncertain.

items: A moon has a variable magnetic signature and a low-density ice shell.
Its plume contains hydrogen, carbon compounds and salts.
A model places liquid water above rock.
What can you claim, and what must still be tested?

panels: Construct a defensible explanation

The magnetic response may support an electrically conducting layer, while the plume reveals accessible chemistry. Together these clues strengthen an ocean interpretation, but interior models can depend on assumed geometry and composition. Hydrogen and carbon chemistry may supply ingredients for energy-yielding reactions. The evidence supports investigating habitability; it does not demonstrate organisms.
Design the next observation

Ask whether the proposed reactants coexist at useful concentrations and temperatures, whether supply is renewed, and whether the sampled plume represents the deep source. Repeated composition measurements, better interior constraints and geological context can distinguish competing models. An unfamiliar world should be reasoned about using the same criteria as the listed ones, without inventing detailed facts about it.
question: Which part is a direct measurement: “hydrogen in the sampled plume” or “a functioning ecosystem in the ocean”?
answer: Hydrogen in sampled plume material is a measurement-based composition result. The ecosystem is not established. Even the connection between a plume sample and conditions throughout an ocean requires modeling.

chapter: Put the clues together: integrated reasoning
title: Combine a transit with a spectrum
deck: An apparently favorable orbit is only the beginning of the investigation.

items: Transit depth is ¼ as large around the same star.
Both planets transit. RV measurements, with their inclinations accounted for, indicate equal masses.
The transmission spectrum has no prominent features.
Infer size and density, then state the atmospheric ambiguity.

panels: Use the quantitative constraints

Transit depth scales approximately as the square of planet-to-star radius ratio. One quarter of the depth therefore indicates half the planetary radius, assuming comparable stellar surface brightness and negligible contamination. At equal planet mass, halving radius reduces volume by eight and raises mean density by eight. That is a bulk constraint, not a unique interior composition.
Keep the spectrum ambiguous

A featureless transmission spectrum may reflect no substantial atmosphere, high clouds or haze, a compact high-molecular-weight atmosphere, insufficient sensitivity, or stellar effects. It does not establish a surface ocean. Report what classes of atmosphere were tested and excluded, together with uncertainty. Use the system’s irradiation and stellar activity to frame hypotheses, not to replace measurements.
question: Why should a transit-depth comparison specify the same star or account for the stars’ radii?
answer: Depth depends on the ratio Rp/Rstar. Equal depth around different-sized stars can correspond to different-sized planets.

chapter: Put the clues together: integrated reasoning
title: Connect energy, gas and chemistry
deck: A single environmental change can have several different consequences.

items: A sealed rigid gas sample follows the new temperature.
What can and cannot be predicted about reaction rate?

panels: Follow the model step by step

In the uniform equilibrium-temperature model, T scales as the fourth root of flux, so the Kelvin temperature doubles. In a fixed-volume ideal-gas container with the same amount of gas, pressure is proportional to Kelvin temperature, so pressure also doubles. These linked results require the stated assumptions; a real atmosphere is not a sealed rigid container and its surface temperature need not equal the equilibrium benchmark.
Know where a ratio is insufficient

For a simple Arrhenius reaction with fixed prefactor and positive activation energy, increasing temperature raises the rate constant. But the increase is not necessarily twofold, fourfold or sixteenfold. The activation energy and initial temperature are required to calculate it. Chemical equilibrium can also change with temperature; a faster rate alone does not tell you the final composition or whether molecules remain biologically functional.
question: Can the factor-of-two temperature result alone determine the Arrhenius rate increase? Explain.
answer: No. The exponential contains activation energy divided by RT, so both the activation energy and the actual temperatures are needed for a numerical rate ratio.

title: Eruption is not the same as sublimation
deck: Compare transport from an interior with direct loss of surface ice.

rows: Volatile-rich material erupts from within a cold body
Vents, deposits, composition, heat and structure
Exposed solid changes directly to gas

panels: Follow the material

Cryovolcanism is eruption of volatile-rich material, such as water or other low-melting-point substances, rather than ordinary molten silicate rock. The erupted material may freeze, vaporize or deposit particles after release. Surface morphology alone rarely identifies the full pathway. Combine landforms with composition, temperature, temporal change and interior evidence to test whether an internal source is plausible.
Do not give every plume the same origin

On comet 67P, solar heating drives sublimation and gas-dust activity; a visible jet does not by itself require a liquid reservoir. Enceladus links its south-polar plume to a subsurface ocean through several independent measurements and models. The visual similarity of two jets is therefore weaker evidence than their chemistry, setting and energy source. Avoid calling all gas loss cryovolcanism or treating all erupted water as evidence of a habitable ocean.
question: Why does a gas-and-dust jet on a comet not establish a subsurface liquid ocean?
answer: Surface or near-surface ice can sublime directly to gas when heated by sunlight. An ocean requires additional evidence excluding or complementing that pathway.

chapter: Put the clues together: graphing evidence
title: Sketch the relationship before solving
deck: These are idealized practice values, not observations of a named world.
panels: Test a model against data

Sketch distance on the horizontal axis and flux on the vertical axis, labeling both as ratios. Plot the four points and add vertical uncertainty bars. An inverse-square model predicts 1, 1/4, 1/9 and 1/16. These predictions are consistent with the rounded practice values. Draw a smooth decreasing curve that becomes less steep, not a straight line joining only the first and last points.
Change the plot to expose the law

Now sketch flux against 1/r². The same ideal model becomes a straight line through the origin. This transformation makes proportionality easier to inspect; systematic departures could reveal measurement bias or missing physics. As a separate exercise, sketch emitted flux against Kelvin temperature for fixed emissivity. Its T⁴ curve rises increasingly steeply. Always identify whether a displayed axis uses r, r², 1/r² or a logarithm before interpreting its slope.
question: On the original distance-versus-flux graph, estimate F/F₀ at r/r₀ = 5 using the model, then explain how the transformed plot helps.
answer: The model gives 1/25 = 0.04. A plot of F against 1/r² should be linear for a fixed isotropic luminosity, making departures from proportionality easier to see.
